course_name_en: Industrial Automation (Mechanical Engineering / Industrial Technologies Engineering / Energy Engineering)
prerequisites: Mathematical and physical fundamentals acquired in basic subjects of the degree
Basic computer skills for user-level personal computer operation
Familiarity with simulation software like MATLAB

learning_outcomes.text: Knowledge of the fundamentals of automation and control methods.

Students have demonstrated possession and understanding of knowledge in a field of study that builds on general secondary education, and is typically at a level that, while supported by advanced textbooks, also includes some aspects involving knowledge from the forefront of their field of study.

Students know how to apply their knowledge to their work or vocation in a professional manner and possess the competencies typically demonstrated through the elaboration and defense of arguments and problem-solving within their field of study.
Students have the ability to gather and interpret relevant data (usually within their field of study) to make judgments that include reflection on relevant social, scientific, or ethical issues.
Students have developed the learning skills necessary to undertake further studies with a high degree of autonomy.
Ability to work in a multilingual and multidisciplinary environment.
Knowledge in basic and technological subjects, enabling them to learn new methods and theories, and providing them with versatility to adapt to new situations.
Ability to solve problems with initiative, decision-making, creativity, critical reasoning, and to communicate and transmit knowledge, skills, and abilities in the field of Industrial Engineering.
Knowledge for carrying out measurements, calculations, valuations, appraisals, expert reports, studies, reports, work plans, and other similar tasks.
Ability to manage specifications, regulations, and mandatory standards.

syllabus_topics: TEMA 1: Introduction to continuous control systems
Types and classification of control systems
Characteristics and requirements of a control system
Transfer functions of some real systems
TEMA 3: Analysis of temporal response. Introduction
Types of inputs and system definition
TEMA 6: Analysis of frequency response. Introduction
Logarithmic diagram of amplitude as a function of phase or Nichols chart
TEMA 8: General concepts of discrete control systems
The computer as a control element
TEMA 10: Temporal analysis of discrete control systems
TEMA 11: Temporal behavior in the Z-plane
TEMA 12: Direct design method for discrete controllers (TRUXAL)
teaching_methods: Participation of the Teaching Team, Tutor Professors, and enrolled students
Theoretical-practical content delivered via the virtual course using basic bibliography and complementary material
Autonomous work with exercises and self-assessment tests under tutor supervision
Practices involving a preliminary exercise and practical activities in departmental laboratories
assessment_rules: The final grade is calculated as: [On-site exam score (if >= 4) + 6.6% * PEC1 score (if > 5) + 6.6% * PEC2 score (if > 5) + 6.6% * Tutorial Report score] * 0.9 + Practices score * 0.1, with a maximum final score of 10 points. The on-site exam has three parts: a 10-question multiple-choice section (3 points, +0.3 for correct, -0.15 for incorrect), which is eliminatory requiring at least 5 correct answers; four short questions (4 points); and one long development problem (3 points). A minimum of 4 points in the on-site exam is required for PEC scores to be considered. Practices are mandatory and must be passed to pass the course; failure to pass practices will result in a maximum final grade of 3. For in-person practices, students must complete and pass remote lab practices beforehand and either pass the multiple-choice section of the on-site exam (5 correct answers) in the current sitting or have passed the on-site exam (5 points or more) in a previous sitting. Grades from practices are saved for successive academic years if the course is not passed.
